response:
Before the bacterium's acceptance, peptic ulcers were widely attributed to stress and excess gastric acid. The prevailing treatment followed from that model: antacids, acid-suppressing drugs, bland diets and, in refractory cases, partial gastrectomy. Although the stress-and-acid account dominated clinical teaching, many gastroenterologists initially doubted that any bacterium could survive in the acidic stomach. To most practitioners, the stomach's low pH made it effectively sterile, so reports of microbes in gastric tissue were dismissed as contamination or as organisms of no clinical consequence. Against this background, in 1979 Warren observed curved bacteria in biopsies of inflamed stomach tissue, an observation that came after early attempts to culture the stomach bacterium had failed because plates were discarded after about two days. Laboratories treated forty-eight hours as the standard window for routine throat and gut specimens, and the slow-growing organism had never been given enough time to appear.

The breakthrough in cultivation came from an interruption to routine. A culture plate left incubating over the 1982 Easter long weekend produced the first successful growth of the bacterium. Only when the organism could be grown reliably in pure culture could it be tested as a deliberate infectious agent, and in 1984 Marshall drank a culture of the bacterium to test whether it could infect a healthy stomach. Because he had ingested the organism, Marshall developed acute gastritis within days of drinking the culture. Endoscopy and biopsy confirmed both the inflammation and the presence of the bacterium, satisfying in a single subject the demand that a suspected pathogen reproduce the lesion it is said to cause. That gastritis, together with the epidemiological and therapeutic studies that followed, is the evidence on which the Nobel Assembly at Karolinska Institutet determined that H. pylori infection causes gastritis and peptic ulcer disease. The Assembly's determination settled the earlier tension: the bacterium does survive in the stomach, and its presence, not stress or acid alone, accounts for most ulcers. The Assembly's conclusion likewise confirms that Marshall developed a bleeding duodenal ulcer as a result of his self-experiment.

The aftermath of the self-experiment is recorded in two incompatible ways. Either Marshall treated his self-induced infection with antibiotics, or his self-induced infection was never treated with antibiotics; the two accounts cannot both be true, and one of them must hold. Whatever the case, the practical lesson for clinicians was that eradication therapy, rather than lifelong acid suppression, offered a prospect of cure. The scientific community ultimately recognized the work at the highest level: Warren and Marshall received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1995.

The clinical consequences of the discovery are visible in ordinary diagnostic reasoning. Consider a patient presenting with a confirmed gastric ulcer, a positive urea breath test, and a history of daily anti-inflammatory medication for arthritis. The clinician must recognize that at least one of two causes is operating, perhaps both: the patient's peptic ulcer was caused by H. pylori infection, or the patient's peptic ulcer was caused by long-term NSAID use. Because these mechanisms frequently coexist, guidelines now recommend testing for the bacterium and reviewing medication in every ulcer patient, rather than defaulting to acid suppression alone. The once-dominant stress model contributes little to such an evaluation.

The recognition of 1995 corresponds, in other words, to the fact that Barry Marshall and Robin Warren shared the 2005 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Equivalently, the 2005 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was jointly awarded to Robin Warren and Barry Marshall. The award honored not a single experiment but a sequence of work: careful histological observation, the persistence required to grow a fastidious organism, a willingness to test a hypothesis on one's own body, and the clinical trials that showed eradication prevents ulcer recurrence. Together these overturned a deeply entrenched consensus and reshaped gastroenterology.
